ABSTRACT
Emotion detection from text is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that enables
systems to identify and classify the emotional state conveyed by written language. This project
presents an Emotion Detection System trained on a large-scale multi-class dataset comprising 106,355
text samples spanning eleven distinct emotion categories: anger, empty, enthusiasm, fun, happiness,
hate, love, neutral, relief, sadness, and surprise.
The system employs a classical machine learning pipeline in which raw text is preprocessed through
lowercasing, punctuation removal, stop-word filtering, and lemmatization using NLTK. Feature
extraction is performed using TF-IDF vectorization with trigram support (n-gram range 1-3) and
sublinear term-frequency scaling across a vocabulary of up to 10,000 features. Two classification
algorithms are trained and evaluated: Logistic Regression with grid-searched regularization and
LinearSVC, both configured with class-weight balancing to address class imbalance.

Model selection is performed via 3-fold cross-validated GridSearchCV, and both models are
benchmarked on a held-out 20% test split using accuracy, per-class precision, recall, F1-score, and
confusion matrices. The system concludes with an interactive prediction loop allowing real-time
inference: Logistic Regression outputs top-3 emotion probabilities while SVM provides a hard-label
prediction.
The proposed system demonstrates that well-tuned classical ML pipelines can achieve competitive
emotion classification performance, offering interpretability and computational efficiency compared to
deep learning approaches.
1. INTRODUCTION
Emotion detection from text is the task of automatically identifying the emotional tone expressed in
written language. As digital communication proliferates across social media, messaging platforms, and
online communities, the ability to automatically infer human emotions from text has become
increasingly valuable in applications ranging from customer sentiment analysis to mental health
monitoring, chatbot development, and human-computer interaction.
1.1 Motivation
Manual emotion labelling is time-consuming and subjective. An automated system that can reliably
classify text into fine-grained emotion categories enables large-scale analysis of user sentiment, early
detection of distress in mental-health contexts, and improved personalisation in conversational agents.
The availability of large, labelled datasets makes supervised machine learning an attractive and
effective approach for this task.
1.2 Problem Definition
Given a sentence or short text passage, the system must assign it to one of eleven emotion classes:
anger, empty, enthusiasm, fun, happiness, hate, love, neutral, relief, sadness, or surprise. The dataset
of 106,355 samples is moderately imbalanced (the 'empty' class contains only 6,358 samples while all
others have approximately 10,000). The challenge is to build a pipeline that is robust to this imbalance
and generalises well to unseen text.
1.3 Existing System
Prior approaches to emotion detection range from lexicon-based methods (e.g., WordNet-Affect, NRC
Emotion Lexicon) that rely on hand-crafted sentiment dictionaries, to deep learning models such as
BiLSTM, BERT, and RoBERTa that capture contextual semantics. Lexicon-based systems are fast but
brittle; deep learning models are powerful but computationally expensive and require large GPU
resources for training. Classical machine learning methods such as SVM and Logistic Regression offer
an effective middle ground: competitive accuracy, fast inference, and full interpretability.
1.4 Proposed System
The proposed system is a classical NLP pipeline consisting of: (1) text preprocessing with NLTK
stop-word removal and WordNet lemmatization; (2) TF-IDF vectorization with 1-3-gram features and
sublinear TF scaling; (3) two classifiers-Logistic Regression and Linear SVM-tuned via grid search with
cross-validation; and (4) an interactive prediction interface that displays top-3 emotion probabilities from

Logistic Regression alongside the SVM hard-label prediction.

Programming Language: Python 3.8 or higher
Libraries: scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, nltk, re (standard library)
Dataset: final_dataset.csv - 106,355 rows, columns: text, emotion
IDE: Jupyter Notebook, VS Code, or any Python IDE
1.5.2 Hardware Requirements

RAM: 8 GB minimum (16 GB recommended for GridSearchCV on full dataset)
Storage: 1 GB free disk space
1.6 Languages and Technologies Used
1.6.1 Python
Python is the core programming language of the project. Its rich ecosystem of data science and NLP
libraries (scikit-learn, pandas, numpy, nltk) makes it ideal for building end-to-end machine learning
pipelines for text classification.
1.6.2 Scikit-learn
scikit-learn provides the machine learning backbone: TfidfVectorizer for feature extraction,
LogisticRegression and LinearSVC for classification, GridSearchCV for hyperparameter tuning, and
train_test_split for dataset partitioning. Evaluation tools (accuracy_score, classification_report,
confusion_matrix) are also sourced from this library.
1.6.3 NLTK
The Natural Language Toolkit (NLTK) is used for preprocessing: the stopwords corpus removes
common English function words, and the WordNetLemmatizer reduces inflected word forms to their
base lemma (e.g., "running" ? "run"), improving feature quality.
2. LITERATURE SURVEY
The following literature survey synthesizes research published between 2019 and 2024 in the domain
of emotion and sentiment detection from text using machine learning and NLP techniques. Studies
were sourced from IEEE, Springer, ACM, Elsevier, and MDPI publications.
2.1 Literature Survey Table

Table 2.1 presents the consolidated literature survey covering reference papers on emotion detection
from text using machine learning and NLP techniques.
The literature survey reveals that transformer-based models achieve the highest accuracy for emotion
detection but require significant computational resources. Classical ML approaches such as LinearSVC
with TF-IDF and Logistic Regression offer a practical balance of accuracy, speed, and interpretability,
making them suitable for deployments without GPU infrastructure.
3. DESIGN METHODOLOGY
This chapter describes the end-to-end design of the Emotion Detection system, covering the overall
system architecture, the data preprocessing pipeline, feature extraction strategy, model training and
tuning procedure, and evaluation methodology.
3.1 System Architecture
The system is structured as a sequential, modular pipeline consisting of six principal stages:
Raw Text Input - User-provided sentences or CSV-sourced labelled text.
Preprocessing Module - Normalisation, punctuation removal, stop-word filtering, and lemmatization.
Feature Extraction - TF-IDF vectorization with 1-3-gram features.
Model Training - GridSearchCV-tuned Logistic Regression and LinearSVC classifiers.
Evaluation - Accuracy, classification report, and confusion matrix on a 20% hold-out test set.
Interactive Inference Loop - Real-time user input with top-3 LR probability scores and SVM label.
3.2 Data Flow Diagram
The data flows as follows: the raw CSV (final_dataset.csv) is loaded into a pandas DataFrame.
Duplicate and null rows are dropped and texts shorter than 3 characters are filtered. The preprocess()
function is applied to every text sample. The cleaned corpus is split 80/20 into training and test subsets
using stratified sampling to preserve class proportions. The training subset is passed to
TfidfVectorizer.fit_transform() and the test subset to vectorizer.transform(). Both transformed matrices
are fed to the respective GridSearchCV objects for classifier training and validation.
3.3 Preprocessing Pipeline
The preprocess() function applies the following transformations in order:
Lowercasing: All characters converted to lowercase to ensure vocabulary uniformity.
Punctuation and Non-Alphabetic Character Removal: A regular expression strips all digits, symbols,
and punctuation marks, leaving only alphabetic tokens and spaces.
Stop-Word Filtering: English stop words from the NLTK corpus are removed, eliminating function words
that carry minimal semantic content.
Lemmatization: WordNetLemmatizer reduces each token to its dictionary base form, reducing
vocabulary sparsity.

3.5 Model Selection and Training
Two linear classifiers are selected for their established efficacy in text classification tasks:
3.5.1 Logistic Regression
Logistic Regression is trained with class_weight='balanced' to compensate for the 'empty' class
imbalance, and max_iter=2000 to ensure convergence. The regularization strength C is tuned over
[0.1, 1, 5] via 3-fold GridSearchCV. Logistic Regression outputs calibrated class probabilities, enabling
the top-3 emotion display in the interactive mode.
3.5.2 Linear SVM
LinearSVC implements a linear support vector classifier optimised with coordinate descent, offering
faster training than the kernel SVM on high-dimensional sparse TF-IDF matrices.
class_weight='balanced' is applied and C is tuned over [0.1, 1, 5] via 3-fold GridSearchCV with
max_iter=3000. LinearSVC produces hard class-label predictions.
